THOUGHT: This 20-year-old female presents with acute onset of auditory hallucinations (voices speaking in third person, making negative comments, and urging self-harm), intrusive thoughts, and concentration difficulties — all emerging *within one week* following the sudden, traumatic bereavement of her father from lung cancer. Crucially, she has no prior psychiatric or medical history, no substance use (confirmed by negative urine toxicology), and normal laboratory workup (CBC, CMP, TSH), ruling out metabolic, infectious, endocrine, or toxic causes of psychosis. Her mental status exam shows preserved orientation, linear thought process, euthymic mood with congruent affect, and fair judgment — arguing against a primary mood disorder with psychotic features (which typically features mood-congruent hallucinations and prominent depressive or manic symptoms, neither of which is present here). While grief can involve transient sensory experiences (e.g., “sense of presence” of the deceased), the current symptoms — particularly third-person auditory hallucinations with command content (self-harm), lack of insight, and functional impairment — exceed typical bereavement-related phenomena. The acute onset (<1 month), presence of prominent hallucinations and disorganized thinking (though thought process is described as linear, the content is clearly delusionally infused by the voices’ influence), and absence of mood episode criteria point strongly toward *brief psychotic disorder*, specifically the “with marked stressor(s)” specifier (i.e., brief reactive psychosis), per DSM-5-TR. This diagnosis requires psychotic symptoms lasting ≥1 day but <1 month, with eventual full return to premorbid functioning — consistent with this presentation. Schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder are unlikely given the acute onset tied temporally to extreme stress, absence of prodromal symptoms, young age at first episode without prior deterioration, and expected remission (per course). Delusional disorder is excluded due to prominent hallucinations (not just delusions) and short duration.

DIAGNOSIS: Brief psychotic disorder, with marked stressor(s)
